analysis.one_liner: Lets you sign up once to block most telemarketing calls to your home.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee or floor vote; it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to build national do-not-call lists, one for each state, so a consumer could sign up once and stop most telemarketing calls. Telemarketers would have to buy only from lists that exclude registered households, keep their own no-call lists, honor evening call curfews, and stop using fax blasts, automated dialers, and caller ID blocking. It also let consumers sue for $500 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Households tired of sales calls, especially at dinnertime. Anyone who signs up would be shielded from telemarketers, including calls designed to harvest information for marketing, and would get a confirmation number when a solicitor agrees to stop calling. The bill would also block the practice of disguising a telemarketer's number so caller ID can't show it.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the FTC to establish and maintain do-not-call lists for each state, and consumers may request to be added and removed.
Bars telephone solicitors from calling any consumer on the FTC lists, on their own no-call list, or between 9 p.m. and 9 a.m. and between 5 p.m. and 7 p.m. local time.
Prohibits fax solicitations, calls made with automated dialing or recorded-message devices, and any method that blocks or circumvents caller ID service.
Requires companies that compile and sell consumer call lists to telemarketers to exclude anyone on the FTC list.

Gives consumers a private right of action with $500 in damages per violation, which courts may triple and couple with attorney's fees for willful violations, plus FTC enforcement as an unfair or deceptive trade practice.

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing companies, which would lose access to millions of households and face per-violation lawsuits, and the list brokers and data compilers who sell them call lists. The FTC is authorized to charge solicitors fees for the lists, and Congress must appropriate funds to run the program.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts tax-exempt nonprofits, political candidates and parties, and referendum campaigns, so calls from charities and political operations would remain legal.

The dinnertime curfew (5 to 7 p.m.) bans calls at hours some consumers would accept, a consumer must affirmatively opt in, and lists update only quarterly, so a newly enrolled number could still receive calls until the next update.

The $500-per-violation private right of action, triplable at a court's discretion, invites litigation against small businesses that make a dialing error, and compliance costs fall on legitimate direct sellers as well as on abusive operators.
The FTC is authorized to charge fees for providing lists, a cost solicitors would pass along in their pricing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: a single opt-out that stops most commercial sales calls, including dinner-hour interruptions, fax blasts, robocalls, and caller ID spoofing. The tradeoffs are modest — charities and political callers are exempt, a quarterly update cycle leaves a brief lag, and the private lawsuit provision risks some litigation against small operators. On balance the consumer protection clearly outweighs the costs, which is roughly the design Congress later enacted when a national do-not-call registry finally launched.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced on December 20, 2001, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up; it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Dodd introduced the bill with Sen. Miller on December 20, 2001, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The bill drew two Senate Democratic cosponsors.
No further action was ever recorded: the committee held no markup and the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telemarketing companies and the list brokers who sell them consumer call lists, which kept operating without these restrictions for the rest of the Congress. Consumers gained nothing from this bill itself, though a national do-not-call registry was ultimately created by separate legislation in 2003.

for.name: Sen. Christopher J. Dodd
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill; it was read twice and referred to committee.

against.name: Sen. Fritz Hollings
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill received no action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by two Democrats with two Democratic cosponsors, but it never reached a vote, so no record exists of how either party or the full committee stood on it.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from calling any household on a national do-not-call list, restrict evening call hours, and ban fax blasts, robocalls, and caller ID blocking, with $500-per-violation lawsuits on top. Their sales channel depends on the calls consumers want stopped, so their interest ran against the public's here.

industries.industry: List brokers and consumer data compilers
industries.note: The bill requires anyone who compiles and sells consumer name-and-number lists to telemarketers to strip out households on the FTC list, shrinking their product's value. They profit from selling access to people who have asked not to be called.
By banning techniques that block or circumvent caller ID, the bill reinforces the value of a service consumers pay for and makes it reliable for screening calls.
